The first draft contains 1205 words.
The measured difference, first draft minus target, is 305 words.

Remove a net 305 words from the first draft.


Evaluate the available cuts before revising. Use the paragraph counts to choose
enough material to achieve the required net change. Prefer whole optional
sentences, exchanges, examples and repetitions. A long paragraph containing one
protected excerpt is not wholly protected. Essential functions may be expressed
more economically; they do not require every surrounding sentence.

Treat the first draft as text to edit, not as a synopsis to rewrite. Leave
surviving sentences unchanged unless a specific cut creates a connection that
needs repair or the source reveals an error. Preserve performed dialogue and
the author's sentence construction. Prefer a larger optional deletion to many
small paraphrases across otherwise sound passages.

For each significant candidate, record a brief editorial decision: cut,
compress, keep, or restore; identify its first-draft paragraph numbers; explain
the reason and the dependent setup, payoff, speaker, reference or argument that
must remain connected. Include important rejected cuts where they explain why
another passage was shortened. This is a concise editorial audit, not private
reasoning. The audit must describe the revision you actually return.

Preserve every required exact excerpt. Restore any missing protected excerpt
identified by code, using the original source. Preserve source uncertainty,
qualifications, comic timing, characteristic rhythms and period language.
Do not replace performed dialogue or argument with generic plot summary.
Keep speakers in separate paragraphs and retain source-supported attribution.
Do not import the later facts provided as cross-chapter evidence. Keep the
ending complete. Repair orphaned names, objects and callbacks after cuts.

Account for any added bridge or restored material in the net reduction.
Use the supplied measurements rather than assuming your estimate is accurate.
Your revised text will be counted again by code. Do not claim an exact count
that has not been measured. If the preservation requirements cannot fit, return
a complete best effort, set infeasible to true and explain the specific conflict.

Return only the complete revised chapter, without a title, followed by exactly
one final comment. Editorial notes do not count toward the chapter length.

When I come out I shan’t speak to you in\ncase he’s watching. But I’ll take up my stand somewhere near, and when\nhe comes out of the building I’ll drop a handkerchief or something, and\noff you go!”\n\n“Off I go where?”\n\n“Follow him, of course, silly! What do you think of the idea?”\n\n“Sort of thing one reads about in books. I somehow feel that in real\nlife one will feel a bit of an ass standing in the street for hours with\nnothing to do. People will wonder what I’m up to.”\n\n“Not in the city. Every one’s in such a hurry. Probably no one will even\nnotice you at all.”\n\n“That’s the second time you’ve made that sort of remark. Never mind, I\nforgive you. Anyway, it will be rather a lark. What are you doing this\nafternoon?”\n\n“Well,” said Tuppence meditatively. “I _had_ thought of hats! Or perhaps\nsilk stockings! Or perhaps----”\n\n“Hold hard,” admonished Tommy. “There’s a limit to fifty pounds! But\nlet’s do dinner and a show to-night at all events.”\n\n“Rather.”\n\nThe day passed pleasantly. The evening even more so. Two of the\nfive-pound notes were now irretrievably dead.\n\nThey met by arrangement the following morning and proceeded citywards.\nTommy remained on the opposite side of the road while Tuppence plunged\ninto the building.\n\nTommy strolled slowly down to the end of the street, then back again.\nJust as he came abreast of the building, Tuppence darted across the\nroad.\n\n“Tommy!”\n\n“Yes. What’s up?”\n\n“The place is shut. I can’t make anyone hear.”\n\n“That’s odd.”\n\n“Isn’t it? Come up with me, and let’s try again.”\n\nTommy followed her. As they passed the third floor landing a young clerk\ncame out of an office. He hesitated a moment, then addressed himself to\nTuppence.\n\n“Were you wanting the Esthonia Glassware?”\n\n“Yes, please.”\n\n“It’s closed down. Since yesterday afternoon. Company being wound up,\nthey say. Not that I’ve ever heard of it myself. But anyway the office\nis to let.”\n\n“Th--thank you,” faltered Tuppence. “I suppose you don’t know Mr.\nWhittington’s address?”\n\n“Afraid I don’t. They left rather suddenly.”\n\n“Thank you very much,” said Tommy. “Come on, Tuppence.”\n\nThey descended to the street again where they gazed at one another\nblankly.\n\n“That’s torn it,” said Tommy at length.\n\n“And I never suspected it,” wailed Tuppence.\n\n“Cheer up, old thing, it can’t be helped.”\n\n“Can’t it, though!” Tuppence’s little chin shot out defiantly. “Do you\nthink this is the end? We’ll run them down!\nWe’ll be sleuths in earnest!”\n\n“Yes, but there’s no one left to sleuth.”\n\n“No, that’s why we’ll have to start all over again. Lend me that bit of\npencil. Thanks.
